name: Amira Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for agreeing to talk. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. My husband said I should do it, since he's always the one with opinions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee excavator operator at a big nickel mine. Mostly I'm on the smaller excavator, digging drains and cleaning up around the pit, while I learn to load trucks on the big one. I'm still slow at swinging the bucket smoothly, and the trainer has me practising on the simulator twice a week. Yusuf, my husband, is an electrician on the same site, so we drive in together, and he teases me if I come home with mud up to my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about like now. Not much has changed at our mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that it was a lot of talk and not much else. I'd say the same to my sisters, and maybe post something at our church's community page about not worrying over things we can't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, AI isn't our problem, nickel is. My husband and I both work at the same nickel mine, so one bad price slump could take both our pay packets in a single letter. The price has been low all year, and there's talk of putting the mine into care and maintenance, which means shutting it but keeping it ready to restart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep training hard on the big excavator so I'm worth keeping. We'd save more, we're at about four months now, and we'd hold off on the new car. And I'd ask Yusuf to look at jobs at the gold mine down the road, so we're not both in one basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not about AI. About nickel and about having both of us at one mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would care and maintenance mean for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a skeleton crew stays, and electricians are more likely to be kept than trainees like me. So Yusuf might stay and I'd go. We'd survive, but it would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your parents think of you going into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father wasn't sure at first, but the pay is good and Yusuf is there. My mother just wanted me close to home and in a job with a pension.

say: It was a **lot of talk**, and not much else came of it.
She'd post on the **church page** about not fretting over what we can't control.
think: **Nickel prices**, not AI, threaten the household.
Both spouses at **one mine** means one slump hits both incomes.
do: Train hard on the **big excavator** to be worth keeping.
Save more, holding off on the **new car**.
Ask her husband to look at the **gold mine** nearby.
feel: **Anxious** about nickel prices and having both jobs at one mine.

fieldNote: Household risk is **concentrated**: both incomes depend on one mine.
**Care and maintenance** talk is a live pressure even with no AI.
She expects a skeleton crew would keep her **husband** before her.

steps.text: Practise on the big excavator simulator twice a week
Hold off on the new car and save more
Have Yusuf apply at the nearby gold mine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots coming in slowly. That's what the older operators already say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should learn what's useful and not panic. At church, I'd say the same, trust in God and do your work well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think trainees like me are the easy ones to cut when machines get smarter. I'll use the AI tools once the senior operators on my crew trust them, not before. Once they've proven themselves, I'll learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and learn every machine I can, the simulator, the excavator, maybe the grader. I'd start using the planning tools on the tablet once others are using them. We'd save harder and stop eating out on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, just a heavy feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maria, the senior excavator operator. She's been here twenty years and always knows what's coming before the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Yusuf's job be safer than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Someone has to wire and fix all the new equipment. His job might even grow, which is a comfort.

At church she'd say **trust in God** and do your work well.

steps.text: Get tickets on the big excavator and the grader

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's... that's when we wanted a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to make sure families are looked after, and that companies shouldn't throw people away. I'd be careful saying it, I don't like politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes by 2031, maybe sooner if the mine shuts. We'd planned to start a family in 2028, and now I'd be choosing between a baby and a buffer. Yusuf's job would last longer, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save every spare dollar to get to a year of savings by 2030. We'd probably delay the baby. I'd ask my parents if we could move in with them for a while to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It feels like someone's taken a plan we had and torn it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the baby has to wait. She'd be upset, but she'd understand. She'd probably offer to help with the deposit if we bought a house near her instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about training for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but it's hard to choose when everything's changing at once. I'd probably wait to see what's still hiring once the robots come.

say: The government must make sure **families are looked after**.
Companies **shouldn't throw people away**, though she avoids politics.
think: Her job goes by **2031**, maybe sooner if the mine shuts.

S2.quote: We'd planned to start a family in 2028, and now I'd be choosing between a baby and a buffer.
fieldNote: The fast picture hits her **family plans** hardest.
She expects her husband's job to **outlast** hers by a few years.
She'd **wait** before choosing a new career, unsure what survives.

steps.text: Save every spare dollar to reach a year of costs by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and then robots in 2034. Better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, and families should plan rather than panic. I'd tell the women's group at church to start talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Yusuf gets more valuable. Five years gives my husband time to become the electrician who fixes the robots, and me time to find my feet. I'd keep digging until the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf would do extra training on automation and control systems next year. I'd keep working and maybe do a course in something like aged care at night, in case. We'd have our first child around 2028 and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I feel I can breathe. There's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why aged care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother was in a home, and the women who cared for her were wonderful. I think people will always want a person holding their hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip home to see my cousins next year. And Yusuf's fishing gear, though he doesn't know that yet.

She'd get the **women's group** at church talking about it.

She'd keep **digging** on the excavator until the robots come.
do: Support her husband's **automation training** next year.
Take a night course in **aged care**, just in case.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to breathe with a path ahead.
S3.quote: Five years gives my husband time to become the electrician who fixes the robots, and me time to find my feet.
fieldNote: The plan centres on her **husband's trade** becoming more valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. A lot can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade to adjust and we should use it wisely. I'd say it at church and to my sisters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be fine. With ten years, I'd have my children, and my husband's trade would carry us while I work out what's next. By 2039 my kids would be in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have our first baby around 2028, and I'd keep working part-time on the excavator until the robots come. Yusuf would get his automation tickets. We'd buy a house near my parents by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. Ten years feels like enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after the excavator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe aged care, maybe stay home with the children for a while. My mother did that, and I don't think it's a bad life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots touch Yusuf's job too, eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. But someone has to check the robot did it right. I trust he'd find his place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would make us choose between a family and safety. Good work, a steady wage and a family around the table is all I ever wanted from the nickel mine. What would help is training that fits around family, and companies keeping on local people as long as they can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples who work at the same mine. There are lots of us. When the mine has trouble, it's not one job, it's the whole household.

headlineQuote: Good work, a steady wage and a family around the table is all I ever wanted from the nickel mine.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old trainee excavator** operator at a nickel mine, married with no children yet.
Her husband Yusuf is an **electrician** at the same mine, so both incomes share one risk.
She's **traditional**, rooted in faith and family, and adopts AI only once proven.
Even in AI Plateau she is **anxious**, because of nickel prices and care-and-maintenance talk.
Her plans revolve around **when to have children** and her husband's growing trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing a choice between starting a family and keeping a buffer.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping **local people** on as long as they can.
